title: What are payback and NPV, and how do they decide investment cases?
description: Why money today is worth more than money tomorrow, and how payback, discounting and NPV help decide whether an investment is worth it.
hook: Payback is how long an investment takes to earn back its upfront cost; net present value (NPV) is the value today of all its future cash flows, discounted for time and risk, minus that upfront cost. In an investment case, payback gives a quick sense of risk and NPV gives the verdict: a positive NPV means the investment earns more than the client's cost of capital, so it creates value. Both rest on one idea you already know: $100 today is worth more than $100 in five years.
body:
Why money today is worth more

Money you have today can be invested and grow. Money promised in the future might not arrive. So when a company spends money now to earn money later, it needs to get back more than it spent, to make up for the wait and the risk. The return it could earn elsewhere on an investment of similar risk is its cost of capital, and that is the discount rate you use.

Payback: the simple version

Payback = upfront cost ÷ yearly cash saving or profit. A machine costing $2M that saves $500k a year pays back in 4 years. It is easy and very common in cases. Its weaknesses: it ignores everything after payback, and it treats a dollar in year four the same as a dollar today. Always compare payback with the asset's life. A 4-year payback on a machine that lasts 3 years is a bad deal; on one that lasts 10, it is probably a good one.

Discounting

To compare money at different times, shrink future money back to today's value: divide by (1 + discount rate) once for each year of waiting. At 10%, $110 next year is worth $110 ÷ 1.1 = $100 today. The discount factors at 10% are worth knowing roughly:

Year1234
Value today of $1$0.91$0.83$0.75$0.68

A dollar five years out is worth about 62 cents today at 10%.

NPV

NPV adds up all the future cash flows, each discounted back to today, and subtracts the upfront cost. If NPV is positive, the investment beats the cost of capital. Back to the $2M machine saving $500k a year, at 10%:

  • If it lasts 10 years, the savings are worth $500k × 6.14 (the sum of the ten discount factors) ≈ $3.07M today, so NPV ≈ +$1.07M.
  • If it lasts only 3 years, the savings are worth $500k × 2.49 ≈ $1.24M, so NPV ≈ −$0.76M.

Same payback, opposite answers. That is why NPV, not payback, decides.

Why timing changes the answer

Two projects each promise $1.2M in total. Project A pays $400k in each of the next three years. Project B pays nothing for two years, then $1.2M in year three. At 10%:

  • A: $363.6k + $330.6k + $300.5k ≈ $995k today.
  • B: $1.2M ÷ 1.1³ ≈ $902k today.

Equal totals, but A is worth about $93k more because its cash arrives sooner.

A useful shortcut: perpetuities

If something pays the same amount every year forever, its value today is the yearly amount divided by the discount rate. $1M a year at 10% is worth about $10M. If the cash grows each year, divide by (discount rate − growth rate): $1M growing 2% a year at 10% is worth $1M ÷ 8% = $12.5M. This perpetuity shortcut is handy for quick valuations in M&A and private equity cases.

How to talk about it

Weak: "It pays back in four years, so we should do it."
Strong: "It pays back in about four years, within the client's five-year target. The equipment lasts around ten years, so at a 10% cost of capital the NPV is roughly $1M positive. The key risk is the savings estimate, so I'd test what happens if savings come in 20% lower."

Common mistakes

  • Deciding on payback alone. It ignores the asset's life and everything after payback.
  • Adding up cash flows from different years as if they were worth the same.
  • Counting profit instead of cash. Use cash flows, and check whether they are before or after tax.
  • Forgetting extra upfront costs and end values. Working capital, installation and any resale value at the end all count.
  • Over-precision. You rarely need a full NPV aloud. A clean timeline of cash in and out, plus a rough discount, usually surfaces the answer.

Practise

1. A $600k system saves $150k a year and lasts 6 years. What is the payback, and is it likely to create value at a 10% cost of capital?

Show the answer

Payback: $600k ÷ $150k = 4 years, leaving two more years of savings. The sum of the six 10% discount factors is about 4.36, so the savings are worth roughly $150k × 4.36 ≈ $653k: a small positive NPV of about $53k. It creates value, but only just.

2. A $1M project returns $400k a year for three years. Payback is 2.5 years. At 10%, what is the NPV?

Show the answer

Present value of the inflows ≈ $995k (as in Project A above), so NPV ≈ −$5k, roughly zero. A quick payback does not guarantee value; here the project only just earns its cost of capital.

3. A business earns a steady $300k a year, with no growth expected. At an 8% discount rate, what is it worth? The seller wants $3M.

Show the answer

Perpetuity value: $300k ÷ 8% = $3.75M. At $3M the price looks attractive, if the $300k really is sustainable.

Where to practise next

Work through the payback and NPV worked examples and the investment framework. Then try the Northwind Hotels case (heat pumps over 15 years) and the Granite Holdings case (choosing projects under a budget cap).
